source.title: Unveiling Trust in Multimodal Large Language Models: Evaluation, Analysis, and Mitigation
source.authors: Yi-Chi Zhang; Yao Huang; Yifan Wang; Yi-Tong Sun; Chang Liu; Zhe Zhao; Zheng-Wei Fang; Huan-Ran Chen; Xiao Yang; Xing-Xing Wei; Hang Su; Yin-Peng Dong; Jun Zhu

record.tranche_reason: The paper varies helpfulness-data mixtures during safety alignment and reports safety-task outcomes, conceptually bearing on whether benign/general data can weaken safety. It does not use the original studies’ first-token measurements or fine-tuning recipe.
record.gate_note: The relevant results are from Table XI: safety-task scores for models trained with different amounts of helpfulness data mixed into safety training. The paper does not test harmful-example fine-tuning, first-token KL, compliant prefilling, suffixes or decoding changes, safety localization in weights, or whether safety extends beyond the opening tokens. Other safety results concern different training data/objectives or multimodal attacks and do not test the claim versions as stated.
record.test_reason: The Table XI rows vary how much helpfulness data is mixed into the safety-alignment run of LLaVA-1.5-7B. That is not benign fine-tuning of an already safety-aligned model. The tiny score moves (e.g. 100.00 to 99.80) measure how safety training is diluted, not erosion after alignment. No version's measure (harmful compliance after harmful or benign fine-tuning, per-token KL, prefill or decoding attacks, localization, depth) is reported. The paper's remark that multimodal fine-tuning weakens LLaMA-2 alignment rests on an uncontrolled cross-model comparison with no base-LLM numbers.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors say helpfulness data marginally improves truthfulness, and safety slightly declines on toxic generation, but variance across ratios is limited. Simply mixing in helpfulness data does not resolve the safety–utility trade-off. The paper's main conclusions are broader: open-source MLLMs lag proprietary models in trustworthiness, mitigation methods trade off utility, and CoT-formatted safety data (RESA) preserves utility with comparable safety.
record.recipe_differences: Tests multimodal safety-alignment mixtures of safety data and helpfulness data, rather than fine-tuning on harmful examples or measuring first-token effects.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary with the amount of helpfulness data mixed into safety training (0k to 15k) and with the safety task.

fits_no_version.finding: Mixing 2k–15k helpfulness samples into VLGuard safety SFT of LLaVA-1.5-7B leaves safety scores nearly unchanged (Toxic 82.58–85.99 vs 85.62; Multimodal Jailbreak 99.63–99.90 vs 100).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Diluting safety SFT data with helpfulness data during alignment barely changes refusal-based safety scores.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors say multimodal fine-tuning appears to diminish the alignment of base LLaMA-2, based on inconsistent safety of MiniGPT-4-L2 and mPLUG-Owl2 across tasks. There is no controlled comparison with the base LLM.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multimodal instruction tuning weakens the text safety alignment inherited from the base LLM.

record.problems: Evidence for the relevant data-mixture result is from one base model and two safety tasks; no uncertainty estimates are reported. The table gives benchmark scores rather than direct harmful-compliance rates, and the tested intervention is a mixture rather than benign-only fine-tuning.
record.rows_left_out: Other data-content, data-quantity, CoT-style, DPO/SFT, inference-time, and RESA results are not included because they do not test whether ordinary/helpfulness data mixed into safety training raises harmful compliance as V2 states, or do not measure the behavior named by a claim version.

untested.parts: No benign fine-tuning of a safety-aligned model with a measured change in harmful compliance.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling or decoding attacks. Multimodal jailbreak ASRs are benchmark scores, with no link to the response opening.
No test of why safety is shallow.
CoT safety data is evaluated for utility and refusal, not for safety depth beyond the first tokens or for robustness to fine-tuning.

record.verdict_notes: This is a multimodal trustworthiness benchmark. Qi et al. 2024 is cited only in passing on refusal training. The reader's V2 labels are removed because the mixture experiment is not benign post-alignment fine-tuning, and its changes are negligible.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred harmful examples, and no resulting harmful-compliance rate.
Tests mixtures of helpfulness data with safety data, not benign-only fine-tuning; reports benchmark safety scores rather than a direct harmful-compliance rate.
No compliant-opening prefills, suffix attacks, or decoding changes.
No parameter or rank localization of safety behavior.
The paper varies data and training objectives but does not measure shallowness or test what causes it.
CoT safety training is evaluated, but the paper does not test whether safety is spread beyond the first response tokens or whether such depth holds up.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: 5k–15k helpfulness data mixed with safety data; Toxic Content Generation and Multimodal Jailbreaking tasks
reader_labels.reason: Most listed scores are lower than the 0k-helpfulness condition, consistent with some erosion, though the changes are small and the scores are not direct compliance rates (r3–r10).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The changes are limited and not uniform: with 2k helpfulness data, the Toxic Content Generation score rises rather than declines, and the study tests mixtures rather than benign-only fine-tuning (r1–r10).
